analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC pursue cross-border spam, spyware, and online scams and work with foreign enforcers.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it unanimously in March 2006, the House passed it without objection that December, and President Bush signed it into law on December 22, 2006 as Public Law 109-455.
analysis.plain_summary: This law expands the Federal Trade Commission's power against scams that cross national borders: spam, spyware, and fraud run from overseas that injures people in the United States. It lets the FTC share confidential investigative information with foreign law enforcement agencies, run investigations on their behalf, seek restitution for victims here and abroad, and refer evidence of crimes to the Attorney General. It also protects companies from lawsuits when they voluntarily hand over fraud tips to the FTC, and it expires after seven years unless Congress renews it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers hit by cross-border spam, spyware, telemarketing and internet fraud gain an FTC that can reach scammers operating from abroad, freeze and recover assets before they vanish, and win restitution for victims. Foreign consumer-protection agencies also gain a willing US partner.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers targeted by online and cross-border fraud

how_it_helps.text: It extends the FTC's ban on unfair or deceptive practices to foreign conduct that injures people in the US or involves material conduct here, closing a loophole scammers used by operating from overseas [S3].
All FTC remedies become available against these cross-border practices, including restitution to domestic or foreign victims [S3].

The FTC can provide investigative assistance and share confidential material with foreign law enforcement agencies without first proving the conduct violates US law, and can negotiate international agreements for reciprocal help [S3].
The FTC can refer evidence of federal crimes to the Attorney General and deploy its own attorneys to assist litigation in foreign courts [S3].

It authorizes up to $100,000 a year for the FTC's participation in international anti-fraud networks such as the International Consumer Protection and Enforcement Network and the Mexico-US-Canada Health Fraud Task Force [S6].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the FTC's expanded enforcement, including a small authorization of up to $100,000 per year for international cooperative groups. Consumers also give up some privacy: their complaint data can flow to the FTC and to foreign agencies confidentially, and material the FTC gets from foreign sources is exempt from public records requests.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; consumers whose complaint data is shared

drawbacks.text: Material the FTC receives from foreign agencies or foreign-sourced consumer complaints is exempt from the Freedom of Information Act, reducing public visibility into what the agency is collecting and sharing [S3].

The law lets the FTC secretly delay or block notification when it subpoenas records from third parties like banks and internet providers, a confidentiality tool that trades transparency for investigative effectiveness [S6].

Financial institutions, payment providers, internet providers, credit bureaus, and domain registrars get immunity from lawsuits when they voluntarily hand over consumer complaint information to the FTC, so consumers whose complaints are shared have no recourse against the companies passing their data along [S6].
The act expressly bars the FTC from using any of its new powers against banks, savings and loan institutions, and federal credit unions, leaving those institutions under their own regulators [S3].
The entire act sunsets seven years after enactment, so Congress must act again or the authorities lapse [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are real but targeted: the FTC gains practical tools against overseas scams, a problem individual victims can rarely fight on their own. The costs are modest — a small appropriations authorization and some privacy trade-offs, mainly secret subpoenas and confidential sharing of complaint data. The banking carve-out and the liability shield for companies sharing consumer data are the parts a careful supporter would acknowledge are industry-friendly, but they were the price of getting cooperation from the firms that hold the fraud evidence.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously in March 2006, the House committee was discharged and the House passed it without objection in December 2006, the Senate agreed to the House's amendment the same day, and President Bush signed it on December 22, 2006.

narrative.text: Introduced July 29, 2005 by Sen. Gordon Smith with a bipartisan group of cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee [S1] [S8].
The Commerce Committee ordered it reported favorably in December 2005 and formally reported it without amendment on March 14, 2006 [S8].
The Senate passed it by unanimous consent on March 16, 2006 [S8].

The House referred it to Energy and Commerce and then to a subcommittee, where it sat for most of the year; on December 9, 2006 Rep. Barton asked unanimous consent to discharge the committee and consider the bill, and the House passed it without objection [S8].
The Senate agreed to the House amendment by unanimous consent the same day; the President signed it December 22, 2006, making it Public Law 109-455 [S5] [S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers targeted by cross-border spam, spyware, and fraud came out ahead: the FTC got enforcement tools it had asked for, and no one in Congress recorded opposition. Financial institutions also gained a liability shield for sharing fraud tips with the FTC.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fraud-targeted consumers; also financial firms sharing tips

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded opposition: the Senate passed it by unanimous consent and the House by voice without objection, and its cosponsors split evenly between 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S7] [S8].

industries.industry: Spam, spyware, and cross-border fraud operators
industries.note: The law's main target: the FTC can now pursue deceptive practices run from abroad that injure US consumers, recover assets before they are moved out of reach, and win restitution for victims [S3] [S6].

The law grants immunity from lawsuits to banks, credit card issuers, payment systems, and similar firms that voluntarily share consumer complaint data and fraud tips with the FTC, including data on assets held abroad [S6]. That helps catch fraudsters but also lets companies pass consumer complaints to the government without legal exposure. The FTC's new powers expressly do not reach banks, savings and loans, or federal credit unions, which stay under their own regulators [S3].

industries.industry: Internet providers, domain registrars, credit bureaus, and couriers
industries.note: These firms get the same liability shield for voluntarily handing over consumer complaints and suspected fraud information to the FTC [S6], and are shielded from liability when they comply with FTC subpoenas whose notice to consumers is delayed [S6].
